title: Spectral Chaos Does Not Determine Quantum Mpemba Crossings
authors: Ri-Hua Zheng, Yang Xiao, Yu Wang, Ye-Hong Chen, Yan Xia
abstract: In a symmetry-restoration quantum Mpemba effect, an initial state with stronger local symmetry breaking can lose that memory faster than a state that starts closer to the symmetric manifold. We test whether this local ordering reversal is organized by chaotic thermalization in a clean U(1)-conserving spin chain, comparing spectral level statistics with crossings of the entanglement asymmetry for the same Hamiltonians. We find that Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (GOE)-like level statistics alone do not determine whether Mpemba crossings occur. Across field textures, GOE-like spectra can occur with or without entanglement-asymmetry crossings, and crossings can also appear away from the GOE reference. A near-staggered detuned control further shows that even an inversion of the total charge-sector coherence need not produce an entanglement-asymmetry crossing. Thus the crossing response is controlled not by spectral chaos alone, but by how local charge-sector coherence enters the reduced density matrix.
summary: This theoretical work examines the relationship between spectral chaos and the quantum Mpemba effect in a spin chain model. The authors demonstrate that while spectral statistics can be calculated, they fail to predict whether an initial local ordering reversal (Mpemba crossing) will occur. Instead, the crossing behavior is shown to depend specifically on how local charge-sector coherence evolves within the reduced density matrix.
main_problem: The study investigates whether spectral chaos, diagnosed by level statistics, is a sufficient condition to determine the occurrence of a quantum Mpemba crossing during symmetry restoration.
main_result: Spectral chaos alone does not dictate the existence of Mpemba crossings; instead, the crossing response is governed by how local charge-sector coherence enters the reduced density matrix.
method: The authors compare two distinct diagnostics—global spectral level statistics (adjacent-gap ratio) against state-resolved measures like entanglement asymmetry and charge-sector coherence inversion depth.
model_or_system: The system analyzed is a clean U(1)-conserving spin chain, modeled by an XXZ Hamiltonian perturbed by a longitudinal field texture ($h_i = \epsilon \cos(qi + \phi)$).
key_observables: Quantum Mpemba Crossing fraction ($f_{cross}$), Entanglement Asymmetry ($\Delta S_A$), and the adjacent-gap ratio ($\langle r angle$).
important_parameters: System size $N$ (up to 20), field texture parameters ($q, \phi$), and time evolution duration $T$.
main_assumptions: The analysis compares results across various field textures (generic vs. detuned-staggered) to isolate the controlling physical mechanism.
figures_summary: Figures compare $\langle r angle$ against $f_{cross}$ for different field types, showing that distinct patterns emerge depending on whether the coherence or asymmetry is tracked.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares three diagnostics ($\langle r angle$, total coherence $C_A(t)$, and entropy-weighted asymmetry $\Delta S_A$) across various field textures to establish a hierarchy of control over the Mpemba crossing phenomenon.
why_interesting: It provides a detailed, quantitative separation between global spectral properties (chaos) and local, state-dependent dynamics (coherence flow), which is crucial for understanding non-equilibrium quantum thermalization.

Figure 3 compares the spectral and QME responses at fixed ϵ = 1. The raw crossing response is texture- selective, not controlled by a universal threshold in ⟨r⟩: generic and staggered textures form the crossing class, while uniform and detuned-staggered textures do not. These classes nevertheless overlap spectrally. The generic and detuned-staggered sets both include GOE-like spec- tra despite opposite crossing responses, and the stag- gered set crosses away from the GOE reference. The generic texture therefore provides a positive structured- field benchmark and the detuned-staggered texture the corresponding negative control.
